title: Chấm điểm cha mẹ · Problems / Solutions
prompt: Some societies are considering requiring new parents to attend publicly funded parenting courses. What problems could this create, and what measures could be taken to address them?
instructions: Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.

paragraphs: Public parenting courses can offer practical help, but funding advice and compelling attendance are different decisions. Compulsory attendance can punish inaccessible participation and stigmatise families; flexible provision and narrowly justified protection requirements offer a more proportionate response.

Compulsory attendance may stigmatise families or ignore cultural and practical differences. Mandatory attendance imposes time and transport costs that differ across households, while a standard course may not fit every family's circumstances. Treating absence as evidence of poor parenting can stigmatise people whose main difficulty is access rather than a lack of concern for their child. A practical demonstration can correct misinformation about infant care, but compulsory attendance may penalise parents whose work or transport arrangements make participation difficult. A parent working rotating shifts may have no stable evening available, while a parent with limited language skills may attend without understanding the advice. Recording both cases simply as successful or failed attendance hides whether the programme has actually helped anyone change a difficult caregiving practice.

Support should be welcoming and flexible, with compulsion limited to clearly justified protection cases. Flexible provision should lower practical barriers before attendance is interpreted as commitment, and any compulsion needs a protection justification beyond the general value of advice. Evening sessions, interpreters and remote questions would help parents use the advice; a missed class should trigger an offer of another appointment rather than an automatic judgement about neglect. Providers should therefore offer alternative times and language support, and invite questions about particular problems, before interpreting absence or silence as unwillingness to care for a child.
Overall, i would favour accessible support as the general rule, reserving compulsory intervention for justified protection cases rather than treating every new parent as a potential failure.
